speechtext:
That is a shocking situation in Canada. There is not a member in this house who does not view with horror a situation of that kind. It is having a profound effect, sir. Every hon. member in this house knows that it is exercising a profound social influence at the present time on the homes of this country.

A release of the dominion bureau of statistics of August 4 contained these interesting figures:
The estimated number of families in Canada in June, 1948, was 3,088,000, an increase of 46,000 over June, 1947, and 562,701 or 22-3 per cent more than at the 1941 census. The average size of family in 1948 was 3-8 persons as compared with 3-7 in 1947 and 3-9 in 1941. In each region, a decline in size of family took place between 1941 and 1948. This is reflected in an increasing proportion of families in the small-size groups, the percentage of families from two to four persons constituting 74 4 per cent of all families in 1948 as compared with 70-8 per cent in this category in 1941.
Every member in this house knows that one of the factors that have entered into that situation is a lack of housing of the kind that Canadian families ought to enjoy.
It is a matter of the most profound shame to this country that the brunt of this problem has been thrown upon the veterans, those to whom this country owes the most.
On this aspect of home ownership, the minister has made some point of assistance to home ownership. We of the Progressive Conservative party believe that there are great social and economic benefits attached to home ownership, and that these are abundant justification for assistance on the part of the government through loans of the kind that we have under part I of the National Housing Act, and other kinds of loans which we hope will be forthcoming under this legislation, in making it easier for people to acquire their own homes; but let us not close our eyes to this inescapable fact, that the high cost of construction today, coupled with emergency conditions faced by many families, has compelled large numbers of Canadians to buy homes, many of which are beyond their means, I am sure; beyond their means, certainly, unless we have in this country an assurance of a high level of employment and a high measure of economic activity in the years ahead.
Let me deal with the subject of housing for rental. There is a need of housing of this kind of great proportions in Canada today. This question of giving assistance in the form of low-cost housing by arrangements with the provinces cannot be adequately weighed, it seems to me, unless the house is also acquainted with the government's plans with reference to rent control. Certainly this whole question of housing for rent is inextricably interwoven with the problem of rent control. I hope that before the debate on the resolution stage js rinsed the government will give a clear statement or announcement in the house as to precisely what it proposes to do with regard to rent control, because there are great numbers of people in Canada who are today living,
National Housing Act
particularly in the overcrowded urban centres, in a condition of great uncertainty as to what faces them on March 31 next, when the present legislative measure expires. If there is to be any attempt to fob off this problem onto the provinces they need adequate warning of that fact. Sir, I reiterate my plea that the government, in fairness to the house, make its intention and its policy in that respect known before this present debate has run its course.
In his statement the minister said that the government has no intention of dealing directly with the municipalities. Nevertheless, the minister is aware that the municipalities are the governments that have had the greatest problem in relation to housing conditions, because these conditions have been literally on the doorstep of municipal governments, and those who have been suffering from lack of housing have, in the first instance, almost invariably gone to their local government pleading for some assistance.
It would profit this house nothing to try at this stage to engage in a discussion on the niceties of the constitutional aspects of responsibility at the three respective levels of government. Whatever may be said about these technical features, the fact is inescapable, sir, that the problem of improving housing conditions is, and has been throughout this entire post-war period, completely beyond the powers of the municipalities to meet. It has been beyond the power of the provinces to meet. They have not had the resources to cope with them, especially when under the emergency powers such wide legislative power has been vested in the government at Ottawa.
Whatever legislation emerges from parliament's consideration of this subject at this session, I hope that we shall keep before us at all times the necessity of preserving the local feature in administration, because the local governments are in the best position to give oversight and effective administration to plans of this kind.
In considering steps that ought to be taken I do say that representations made by such bodies as the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities are entitled to respect, to have great weight attached to them in this house. This association is composed of those representatives of the people in their municipal governments who have had this problem literaily on their doorsteps day in and day out throughout the entire post-war period. Many of the suggestions put forward by the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities to the government have had very great weight, and I am inclined to suspect

National Housing Act
[DOT]that they had some effect in moving the government to take action of the kind that they are taking at long last as contemplated by the present legislation.
When we are talking about assistance to the municipalities I hope, sir, that we have taken some considerable step forward since those days not very long ago when unhappily this government was saying to the municipalities:	"We will not contribute to the
solution of your problem. We are not going to be parties to any subsidy. Any assistance we give to clearing up improper and substandard conditions in any part of this country will be confined to contributions under section 12 of the housing act"-very limited contributions indeed. There is no provision of assistance there toward anything but the assembling of land. Well, sir, at the same time this government, by its policies as administered through Wartime Housing Limited, was literally compelling municipalities to contribute subsidies to the cost of housing erected by that dominion agency, compelling the municipalities which had no choice in the matter, because they had to have housing, and Wartime Housing Limited was, in those days, the only place that they could get housing for rent. That government agency dictated the terms that the municipalities should contribute subsidies in the form of contributions of land and provision of services; yes, and if that was enough, by exacting, in lieu of taxes, payments that very often were little more than a half or a third of the taxes that these same properties would have borne had they not been owned by a government agency.
These municipalities, sir, have had a very unfair share of the load to carry all these years, because the influx to our great urban centres was not the result of any deliberate policy on the part of these municipal governments. The influx into the urban centres occurred in the course of expansion of war production, the result of federal policies almost exclusively; and these municipalities were not in a position financially to meet the need on the scale that then emerged. They were always faced with the possibility that, with the curtailment of war production, there might be an exodus of industrial workers from their areas. In many municipalities, even those that have enjoyed the most rapid growth in these post-war years, there has been a great deal of uncertainty as to how long they could expect it to continue. That has been an additional reason, sir, why the municipalities could not be expected, and were in no financial position, to cope with the problem.
What is government policy with regard to assistance? I am bound to say, sir, that we

have not yet a clear and unequivocal statement of government policy in this country. There was nothing lacking in clarity, there was nothing unequivocal in the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in Montreal on October 27, 1947, when he said this:
No government of which I am a part will ever pass legislation for subsidized housing.
He was quite content at that time that the government of which he was a member should compel municipalities to contribute subsidies if they wanted low-rental housing built; but he was not prepared at that time to be a member of any government that itself made any contribution to subsidized housing, or would pass legislation for subsidized housing.
It has not been made clear in the vague statement made by the minister on September 21, or in his brief statement in the house tonight, whether the government is still adhering to the policy declared by the Prime Minister, or whether there is in the legislation now about to be introduced some assistance to housing by way of subsidy. We are still waiting for a statement in that regard. At page 119 of Hansard for September 21 the minister talks about public-sponsored housing projects as being within the intent of the government to assist by this new measure. But we are still wondering what this policy is.
We find a good precedent for courageous action, in the neighbouring country to the south of us, in meeting the housing problem as it exists over there. In July last President Truman signed a bill which had been passed by congress, and which embraced these five leading features:
1.	A slum clearance program in which the federal government will put up $1 billion in loans and another $500 million in grants to assist localities.
2.	A low rental housing program to be handled by local authorities, designed to provide 810,000 units in the next six years and commit the federal government to annual maximum subsidies of $308 million over a 40-year period.
3.	A broad housing research program designed to improve the construction of housing, and at the same time reduce costs.
4.	Farm housing aids providing for loans and in some cases grants to improve and rehabilitate farm dwellings with the federal government commitment estimated at $325 million.
5.	A 60-day extension as from last June 30 of temporary authority for the government to insure loans by private lenders up to $2,500 for repairing and remodelling existing structures; a 60-day continuation of authority

to insure mortgages for construction of small homes up to $5,000; and a $500 million increase in the amount of mortgage insurance that the government can issue for singlefamily and multiple-dwelling units.
Thinking in terms used by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in the house in recent days, I suppose we could say that half a loaf is better than no bread. At the present time the best one can say about the statement by the minister on September 21, and his statement tonight, and after reading the resolution before the house, is that at best it looks no better than half a loaf, in comparison with the whole loaf promised by the government during the election campaign.
An examination of this resolution discloses that it falls into four parts, and, without risking wearying the house, I shall speak briefly about it.
The first part of the resolution has to do with the assembly of land for residential purposes and the construction of housing projects for sale and for rent under arrangements by which the capital costs and the costs of operation of such project will be shared 75 per cent by the federal government and 25 per cent by the provincial governments in projects undertaken jointly by them.
I believe the minister is quite justified in saying that no pressure should be brought to bear upon the provinces to compel them to enter into projects of this kind. Nevertheless, I affirm that every encouragement should be given to provinces to embark with the federal government upon co-operative measures of this kind. One can welcome this evidence of co-operation between the dominion and provincial governments. For years we have been waiting for the dominion government to appreciate the necessity for seeking co-operation with the provincial governments in addressing itself to this housing problem. And at long last we can welcome this present evidence of willingness on the part of the federal government to cooperate with the provincial governments.
May I say personally to the minister that, to the extent that he has been responsible for this change of front and this change of heart on the part of the government of which he is a member, I congratulate him-and I believe the whole country will congratulate him- most heartily. It is the only approach that promises the massing of the governmental resources of this country to meet that portion of the problem which is a governmental responsibility.
I have one or two further observations to make. The minister's statement of September 21 went farther than his statement of tonight.
National Housing Act
I trust that does not mean that the government has receded from the scope of the legislation which on September 21 he indicated its desire to introduce. On that date the minister indicated a willingness on the part of the government to look into the problem arising from the shortage of serviced land in the municipalities, and the problem which arose through lack of tax revenue from properties owned by the government or its agencies. In urban centres $600 would be a very modest amount to provide services for a dwelling unit. As a matter of fact in many places in Canada it must be very much more than that. This has been an almost prohibitive cost, so far as most municipalities are concerned that have to face this housing problem within their own borders.
On the subject of payment in lieu of taxes, I hope that before this debate has run its course the Prime Minister, or someone on behalf of the government, will make the statement the government has promised to make as to its policy on this subject. We know the British North America Act has the effect of exempting properties owned by the crown in the right of the dominion from either provincial or municipal taxation. But this does not prevent contributions by the federal government or its agencies, equivalent to what the taxes on those properties would be.
Here is a problem from which there is no escape. These municipalities cannot see more and more of their land falling under dominion ownership, or ownership of dominion government agencies, without feeling the effect of this cramping of their limited tax base. If the government is going to meet this problem at long last, I am sure the House of Commons will welcome it; but the house will want the assurance that the government is not going to meet it in the way they used to tell us they were meeting the problem when they were permitting Wartime Housing Limited to make very limited contributions in lieu of taxes-contributions that very often were not half or even a third of the taxes the same property would have borne had it been in private hands.
On September 21 the minister made reference to the necessity of giving more assistance through the act to co-operative house building, but in his statement tonight he made no reference to that. The resolution is silent in so far as any assistance to co-operative house building is concerned. It seems to me, however, that this new measure will be sorely lacking if there is not some provision in it to make the present provisions of the act more useful than they have been in the past-because in the past their usefulness has been completely limited. If one looks at

National Housing Act
what has been done in the way of co-operative house building in other countries, and he will think naturally of Great Britain and Sweden, he will see that in times past our government has overlooked a real opportunity.
Before I leave this subject of joint action and joint contribution on the part of the dominion and the provinces, may I recall to members of the house that the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities, after studying the statement made by the minister on September 21, urged that for at least the first three years of this period the dominion government should go further and encourage a greater measure of participation in the program throughout the country by assuming one hundred per cent of the cost for that period. The recommendation of the federation was as follows:
The federation, therefore, urges the federal government for the first three-year period following the enactment of its low-rental housing policy, to assume the full costs involved in projects commenced during this period; and, thereafter, to require provincial financial participation to the amount of 25 per cent of the annual deficit costs of any further low-rental projects which may be commenced. And, moreover, that, during this three-year initiation period, the federal government, in those municipalities where no approved local housing authority exists, proceed itself to construct demonstration low-rental housing projects.
Having regard to the informed source of that recommendation I think the minister should be asked by the house to give it serious consideration and to make a statement as to whether the government will accept it, or, if not, why not.
The second aspect of the resolution is found in these words:
-and further to authorize the making of loans to prospective home owners in addition to basic joint loans under the act, in amounts not exceeding one-sixth of such basic loans.
That problem can be clearly understood because it concerns the difference between the cost of construction of a new home and the mortgage available today under part I of the National Housing Act. It will not be forgotten that it is federal legislation that creates that problem, that is, section 4, subsection 2, paragraph (c) of the National Housing Act. I have said before that there has been far too rigid and unsympathetic administration of the National Housing Act. In determining the loan value, regard has not been had for the high cost of construction; the percentage which has been authorized under part I of the act has not been based on the high cost of construction; it has been determined by the government agency administering that legislation. That is how that problem of the onerous difference between the cost of construction and the mortgage loan arose.

Ontario, under an enlightened Progressive Conservative government, addressed itself one and a half years ago to that very problem because of a lack of action on the part of the government at Ottawa. Why should any province have had to find a solution for that problem, seeing that the problem was well within the legislative competence of this parliament to solve? The federal government was well equipped with funds and surpluses to meet the financial side of the problem, but there just was not enough sympathetic regard on the part of the government opposite for the extent of the housing crisis in Canada to make them undertake resolutely to find a solution.
What the government of Ontario did was to pass legislation under which provincial loans up to a maximum of $1,250 were made available under second mortgages, or one-half of the difference between the mortgage loan under the act and the cost of construction. The provincial government attempted to fill in the gap created by the dominion government.
What the government is now proposing by this legislation is simply to undertake to do what the government of Ontario has been doing for the last one and a half years. One will welcome this prodigal home. At long last one can say that we welcome the adoption by this government of a good example even though they waited one and a half years to follow it.

speechtext:
I can assure some of the restless hon. gentlemen opposite that I shall not be long, but I do not intend to spare the feelings of the supporters of the government any more than I have been.
I welcome this indication that the government at long last intends to follow this good example. Hon. members will wish to know why it has taken the government one and a half years to decide to follow this example. Hon. members will wish to know why this government has permitted this problem to exist, not only for one and a half years but prior to that time as well. This problem was pointed out to the government in this house in sessions prior to 1947. Of course they were smug, they were satisfied just as they are today, and they followed the course of just letting the people who were faced with the housing problem worry about it.

The other two features of the resolution probably do not require extended comment. I assume provision will be made to increase the amounts now named in the act to cover assistance for home improvement and home extension, and then a consequent provision for increase under Part I of the act by reason of the second feature of the resolution.
There is one other aspect of this problem which I hope will not be lost sight of, the necessity of encouraging research. Ways must be found of lowering the cost of construction, and research must be carried on with a view to improving methods of construction. There is a limit to what the people in the different municipalities want in the way of standardization in construction, but none the less, under conditions such as we face today and in view of the high cost of construction, research into methods of standardized production and various types of housing must be encouraged.
Perhaps it is not amiss to commend the example set by those municipalities which have taken advantage of the present opportunity to re-examine their building codes with a view to determining, in the light of increased knowledge made available through research, how those codes can be changed to take advantage of new and improved methods, at the same time making it easier for people to build houses.
Again I commend to this government the example of the Ontario government, to which I have referred, which in its legislation of one and a half years ago did not stop at the feature I have already mentioned but went farther to meet other aspects of the housing need. I take advantage of the opportunity to remind hon. members that the head of that forward-looking, progressive government which brought in that legislation was the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). That shows what can happen in a province which is blessed with good government under a Progressive Conservative leader.
With all due respect for other provincial governments, Mr. Speaker, you do not find them taking resolute measures of the kind I have referred to. What are these measures which I commend to the attention of the government and invite them to copy? I referred to the first feature, meeting the need for additional mortgage financing by way of second mortgage. The second feature was provision for financing approved building developments where a new method of construction is applied resulting in a substantial reduction in the cost of housing. Under that provision guarantees of up to $2 million were offered.
National Housing Act
The third feature was participation with municipalities in the financing of redevelopment including slum clearance, where this appeared to be a sound policy. That provision was designed to provide rental accommodation on a larger scale, and sums up to $15 million were allocated for that purpose.
Let me just interject here that it was under these provisions that the now well-known Regent Park development was undertaken in the city of Toronto. Limited assistance- altogether too limited-was given by the federal government under section 12 of the housing act in connection with the assembly of land, and I remind hon. members that this housing project was commended by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he went to Toronto and viewed it on February 21 last. At that time he called it "a landmark in Canadian housing"; and that was made possible by legislation of the province of Ontario introduced, as I have said, by a forward-looking, progressive and intelligent government.
The fourth feature of that Ontario program was an offer to pay one-half the cost of lands and services up to a limit of $300 per house, for a tentative ten thousand houses under municipal low-rental projects.
It will probably interest hon. members to learn that since this legislation came into operation one and a half years ago 10,000 mortgages have been approved and sums have been advanced in excess of the $10 million originally appropriated, so that an additional appropriation of $5 million was made available to carry on this worthy endeavour to meet the housing problem.
Always in connection with a problem of this kind there must be something more important than the terms of any legislation that may be passed by this parliament. That is the spirit put into the administration and enforcement of such legislation by the government charged with the duty of administering it. The drive necessary to derive the utmost benefit from existing housing legislation has been woefully lacking in this country in recent years. We had to complain as early as 1945, when different departments had this problem all tangled up. At least three departments were playing with it then; and whatever steps were taken to improve the government's approach to the problem-and I say this without the slightest fear of contradiction-were taken in every case in response to suggestions and demands that came from His Majesty's loyal opposition in the last house.
If this government is to make a serious effort to carry out the promises it made to the people during the election campaign we shall expect it to put behind this new program, or this addition to the old program, such drive

National Housing Act
and vigour as unfortunately it has not yet put behind the housing legislation this parliament has enacted. I am sure nothing but the most sustained drive to make this legislation fruitful in the production of homes for Canadians will satisfy this parliament and the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief. I offer no apology for being proud of what the young minister has done since coming into office. He has shown one of the qualities of a true statesman; that is, co-operation. In the animal kingdom, you know, any animal not willing to co-operate soon passes on. We have the horse, the cow, the sheep and the goat today because they were willing to co-operate for the good of all; and that is just as true of the politician and statesman. If he is willing to co-operate with others who are striving for the betterment of mankind he will have plenty of friends.
I also congratulate the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) on his speech. He always makes a good speech and always has something to say. The statement of the minister this evening was short, just as the down payment that will be required from these young householders will be small. He said a great deal in a very short time. During the summer months, instead of going with his wife and family to enjoy a cool holiday, he was holding conferences with representatives of the provincial governments. On the strength of those conferences we made certain promises; I know I said that if I were not mistaken the minister would bring this matter to a head, and he has done so. Don't I remember how I had my hair pulled, figuratively, when the dominion government stepped into this provincial housing scheme to build wartime houses. I was told very pointedly that a year after the war they would be a burden on the cities in which they were built. I am as sure now as I was then, Mr. Speaker, that it was not a mistake. Perhaps I am more sure now. Those houses are worth more today than they were then. Of course, I do not give the minister credit for seeing that far ahead. When this statement was made by the minister, I know young householders who started saving because they wanted to have a home of their own. They wanted to pay for it. I think the minister is wise, therefore, in requesting that the debate on this matter be not too lengthy. We should have it right away. I know I have had a heart-burning when a young husband and wife with one, two or three children have been unable to find a house. Let us have this thing, and have it right away. As we would say to the old Ford, "Let us step on 
the gas." This measure should be enacted as quickly and as thoroughly as possible. I commend the minister for it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought when the member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) began speaking the minister had done so well in the matter of housing that nothing further need be done. By the time he had finished, he had come to the conclusion it was time to do something. Ordinarily, I am not in favour of extended debates on the resolution stage of a measure. I do not think it is the proper time to have a debate because we do not know the contents of the bill that will be founded upon the resolution. I am going to depart from that rule tonight in view of the great importance and urgency of the question which we are now discussing, the question of housing.
If the proposed bill is of sufficient scope to meet the housing needs, it will be welcomed by the people of Canada as no other measure will be welcomed which this government may propose at this session. I am going to trespass on the time of the house because I do not believe the proposed bill will be of sufficient scope to meet the housing needs of the people of Canada. I am basing that opinion on the resolution itself, on the statement the minister made on September 21 outlining the government's intentions, and the addition to that statement which he made tonight. I do not believe that what is proposed will come anywhere near meeting the situation. It is not my intention to criticize as much as it is to try to show the minister and the members of the house the urgent need for housing which exists in every part of Canada. It is a need which is beyond the ability of the individual family, the ability of the municipality, or the ability of the province to deal with adequately.
I admit at once that there are some good points in the resolution and the proposals contained in the two statements. Despite the fact that constitutionally housing is a matter for the provinces, the federal government is assuming a responsibility perhaps greater than it has assumed up to now; that is all to the good. There is the hope, which I hope is well founded, that the provinces will cooperate and that the municipalities will also co-operate so that we can have a housing development participation by the three governments. Up until now the provinces, perhaps for sufficient reasons in most cases and insufficient reasons in some cases, have refused to co-operate in the matter of low-rent housing.
Another important point is, of course, that the federal government is assuming the major share of the financial burden. The fact that the government hopes to use the co-operative

movement is also a good omen. From the concluding paragraph of the minister's statement on September 21, I do not believe that the government itself has yet realized the amount of assistance, not only the amount of assistance but the amount of initiative, that will be required before the problem is solved. The concluding paragraph of that statement reads as follows:
The policy as enunciated by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply in 1946 is the keystone of our present policy; that is, the creation of conditions favourable to a large housing program by private individuals and companies. Only to the extent that housing needs are not being met is it proposed that the dominion and the provinces will enter the field.
Now, if that is the government's policy up until now, they might as well have no policy at all so far as sixty-five per cent of the people who need houses in Canada are concerned. If there is anything that should be clear to the government by this time, it is that private enterprise will not or perhaps cannot provide houses for those who need them most. During the past four years this has been tried, there has been complete failure despite all the assistance and encouragement the government has given private enterprise.
That the minister himself has doubts of private enterprise's ability to provide the housing needs of the people, I think is made clear by the concluding words of the paragraph I have just read. They are as follows:
It seems to me that only by the co-operative efforts of all levels of government and the house building industry can we maintain our high volume of new residential construction and increase it beyond its present level.
That is not consistent with the first part of the statement which says that the government will only step in when private enterprise has failed. Perhaps this is an afterthought that the government is now going to try to co-operate with the provincial governments and with private enterprise. I am not hopeful of results even in that way.
Let me point this out. I believe there is abundant evidence to prove that private enterprise can build homes for only those who can pay high prices. In the city of Vancouver last summer there were between three hundred and four hundred houses ready for occupancy at one time seeking buyers. Those were homes in the $10,000 to $40,000 class. But the people who need homes in Vancouver cannot purchase houses at those prices, and they could not purchase them even if the down payment were reduced. As a matter of fact, they could not purchase those homes even if there were no down payment at all, because they could not make the monthly payments that would be required
National Housing Act
on houses of that price. That is the problem that is facing the people of Canada and that is the problem that is facing this government.
I should like to quote from various statements from individuals and organizations evidence showing the urgent need for housing in this country. Before I do so, however, let me draw the attention of the house to some figures that were given in an article by Professor Leonard Marsh in the Canadian Journal of Economic and Political Science of February, 1949. The title of the article is "The Economics of Low Rent Housing." The writer says that no family should try to build a house or to buy a house costing more than twice the annual family income. He then pointed out that on that basis 20-7 per cent of those needing homes cannot afford to buy any kind of house; that the next 12-7 per cent cannot afford to buy a house costing more than $3,000 to $4,000; that the next 20 per cent cannot afford to buy a house costing more than from $4,000 to $5,000; and that the next 12-1 per cent cannot afford to buy a house costing more than from $5,000 to $6,000. Here you have 65-5 per cent of those requiring houses in Canada who cannot afford to buy houses priced higher than $6,000.
In my part of the country few houses are being built today which cost less than $6,000. I doubt if any houses at all are being built for less than that. There may be perhaps some three-roomed houses being built for less than that, but I do not think that a house of more than three rooms can be built in western Canada-that is, if it is a modern house-for less than $6,000.
I now want to point out the situation in Vancouver. In a submission made to this government by the Vancouver housing association under date of February 18, 1949, I find the following:
Owing to the tremendous influx of population, the housing situation in British Columbia, already serious at the close of the war, has steadily deteriorated during the last three years, in spite of the relatively high rate of building activity.
In the city of Vancouver alone, the number of houses built has fallen over 2,000 short of the estimated increase in the number of families in each of the last two years.
2. It has become impossible, as a result, to enforce even a minimum standard of health regulations, and slum conditions are steadily spreading outward from the core of our cities.
It is unnecessary to stress the cost, not only in terms of family misery, but in dollars and cents for the community, brought about by these conditions, with their inevitable consequences of ill health, broken homes, juvenile delinquency and social unrest, involving in turn high hospital, penitentiary, police, fire, social assistance and other welfare expenditures.
After the election, along with some other members of parliament representing Vancouver constituencies, and directed by the

National Housing Act
manager or secretary of the Vancouver housing association, we visited some of the worst tenements in the city. We did not visit a great many; we did not have the time to do so. But I am sure that those who were with me will agree that none of the tenements we visited were fit for human habitation. Yet there were families, including young children and old people in large numbers, in those slum tenements.
In a statement issued as late as September, 1949-that is, just last month-the Vancouver housing association mentioned those conditions:
A survey of 1,000 lodging houses by the city health department early this year revealed the following facts: 14-7 per cent of all occupied accommodation were basement or attic rooms; 133 rooms had no window or skylight. Half the lodging houses contained children. There was an average of one bath or shower to every eight persons. In 10 per cent of the houses, there was only one toilet for eleven or more persons. In 20 per cent of the cases the plumbing was graded as poor, in 371 per cent fair. Thirty-two and one-half per cent of the houses were in poor structural maintenance.
Then the statement goes on to say:
One of the most significant points brought out by these tours-
It referred not only to the tours of members of parliament but to those by aldermen of the city as well.
-is the inevitable tendency for the low income families with children to gravitate to the worst accommodation, and it is, of course, just these families who suffer most harm from bad housing and environment.
I am not over-drawing the picture in Vancouver. Vancouver is of course-depending on the parts of it you visit-a city of beautiful homes. Perhaps in no other city of Canada can you find so many beautiful and fine-looking homes; but perhaps in no other city of Canada can you find slums that will compare with ours. The people in my city are therefore concerned about housing. So far as I have been able to learn, they are not satisfied with the proposals made by the government up to now. While those proposals are an improvement over what has been done to date, the people do not believe that they are sufficient to meet the need.
The next publication I want to quote from is entitled "Layout for Living". It is the official organ of the Community Planning Association of Canada with head offices in Ottawa. This publication is speaking for the whole of Canada in the matter of housing. On page 3 I find the following:
In every province there are thousands more families wanting accommodation for rent than there are dwellings to be rented. True, the federal government has built tens of thousands of rental houses since the war-but they are all for veterans. The only houses being added now to the rental supply (and open to all families to try for)

are renting at $50, $60, $70 and up per month. The federal government has offered guarantees to private builders if they will do more rental housing, but even with this it seems almost impossible to get a new apartment to pay for itself if the rent is less than about $70. Yet two-thirds of the urban families in rented shelter in 1948 were paying no more than $30.
These are dominion bureau of statistics' figures.
For this important group of Canadian families- about one in every four of all our families-very little housing has been built since the depression.
That is the situation I should like the minister and hon. members to visualize. I am satisfied that if hon. gentlemen critically approach the problem they will come to the conclusion that the legislation before us is not adequate to deal with it as it should be dealt with.
The next quotation I should like to read is a statement by the chairman of the federation of mayors and municipalities, which appears in the Vancouver News-Herald, of August 31, 1949. Mayor George C. MacLean of St. Boniface, Manitoba, said:
Canadians would be greatly disappointed if the only result of the recently concluded trans-Canada housing tour is to be some sort of federal-provincial arrangement to reduce the required down payment for home purchases.
There he was referring to the housing tour made by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters). I continue:
This is no solution to the housing problem at all. It simply means a lower initial payment- but a higher annual carrying charge. It will encourage some people to begin buying their homes, but it offers no relief to that large aggregation of average workers who, even if no initial equity were required, would still be unable to finance the cost of a minimum standard low-cost home.
He continued:
Broadly speaking the maximum which the average worker's family can afford to put out for shelter does not exceed $25 a month and as the facts show, many can't afford even this.
Compare that wilh the statement in the Canadian community planning association booklet where the rents are from $50, $60 to $70 and up per month and you will appreciate at once why the working people of Canada can find no comfort in the proposals made by the government.
The next publication I wish to quote from is the report of the Canadian welfare council, 1948. On page 5 I find the following:
A word first about living costs where the index now stands at 153 [DOT] 3.
That was in 1948. It is much higher now. I continue:
Agencies in our family division during the past winter attempted to evaluate what was happening to families under their care. The report of this study shows a sharp increase in the number seeking assistance to pay for food, clothing and essential medical and dental care. More mothers are going

to work to help make ends meet with a consequent neglect of children. Increased debts, problems in caring for aged members of the family, older children leaving school for blind-alley jobs, and friction within families, were all reported by most agencies.
And second a comment on housing which is still to be regarded as Canada's number one social problem. Here the point to emphasize is that, although a record number of houses was built in 1947, our national position today is hardly less serious than it was a year ago; nor, if the number of families continues to increase at present rates, are we likely to be any better off next year than we are now.
That situation has not improved in any way whatsoever since this report was published.
At the first session this year I put some questions on the order paper, and they were answered in the form of a return which is to be found in Votes and Proceedings No. 38, for the first session, 1949. The information was given by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. My first question was:
How many houses (family units) were built in Canada in the year 1948?
The answer was:
Housing units built in Canada in 1948 numbered 81,243 including 5,146 housing units added by conversion.
My second question was:
How many houses (family units) were constructed with financial assistance under the provisions of the National Housing Act, during the same year?
The answer was:
The number of housing units completed in 1948 with financial assistance under the provisions of the National Housing Act numbered 11,939.
Hon. members will see the small number of people who took advantage of the National Housing Act. The great majority of those who buy or build houses do not need the assistance of the National Housing Act.
My third question was:
What was the total amount of financial assistance?
The answer was:
The total amount of financial assistance through loans approved under the National Housing Act in 1948 amounted to $101,642,194.
Or an average of $8,512 per family unit.
My fourth question was:
How many houses (family units) were built for rental?
The answer was:
It is estimated that 25 per cent of all housing units completed in 1948 were built for rental (Housing Bulletin No. 12, dominion bureau of statistics, page 3). Those built in 1948 with financial assistance under the National Housing Act numbered 1,599.
The need today, Mr. Speaker, is for rental houses. In 1938-39, 45 per cent of the houses built were for rent. In 1948 only about 30 per cent were built for rent, and the greater proportion of them were veterans' houses; therefore not more than 13 per cent of the houses built were rental houses. My time has almost expired, but, as I said before, I want to give
National Housing Act
the minister and the house the feeling as I find it in my city and province and also as it appears to me throughout the country. Despite any criticism I have made, I do not wish to conclude my remarks without expressing my appreciation of the intention of the government as indicated by the minister to assume 75 per cent of the cost of low-rental housing, in co-operation with the provinces.
Again the question is: Will the provinces co-operate? I believe the premier of British Columbia stated in the legislature early this year that he would be willing to co-operate with the federal government. I believe also that the city of Vancouver acquired the legislation necessary to set up a housing authority. It would appear therefore that at least in British Columbia there can be co-operation on the three levels of government.
If our people are to be adequately housed, in my opinion and in the opinion of all those authorities whom I have quoted tonight, there is no alternative to government assisted housing, except a more equitable distribution of the national income, so that more people will receive incomes which would permit them to build their own homes out of savings over a period of time or out of current earnings.
I mention that possible alternative-but there is no hope at the present time that we shall see a more equitable distribution of income. As a matter of fact there is a growing resistance to wage increases. Let me in concluding tell the house that we must make up our minds that if we do not pay for decent housing for those who cannot provide homes for themselves we shall pay for the poor homes in which they are compelled to live. Perhaps I cannot put that point better than it was put by the citizens committee on housing in Halifax, Nova Scotia, not so long ago. This is what they said:
Housing of the poor we are going to provide, let us make no mistake about that. It is only a question whether we shall house them in hospitals, mental institutions, reformatories and jails; or whether we shall house them in cleanly, light and sanitary surroundings where both body and soul will have a chance. Which shall it be?
I have taken up the time of the house to place these matters before the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) in the hope that, if he has not drafted the bill to be founded on this resolution, he will give consideration to what I have said. If he has drafted the bill I hope he will scrap the draft and prepare a new bill which will more adequately meet the need of homes for the people of Canada.

This year's housing production will be higher than ever before. It is likely to reach a record high of approximately 100,000 units in 1949.

I was interested the other day in an article appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of October 13, 1949, which makes reference to the number of houses built in Canada and states that there are 46,326 more families in their own homes. The article I am about to read does not confine itself to operations under the National Housing Act, but refers to the total number of homes built, and goes on to say:
The first seven months in 1949 saw another 46,326 families in their own homes, a 10,000-home improvement over the housing progress of a year before.
This was reported by the bureau of statistics yesterday in its monthly housing bulletin. It showed however-
And take note of this-
-that fewer new homes were started this year than last. Starts during the seven months of 1949 totalled 49,285 compared with 49,452 in the first seven months of 1948.
The minister is going to have to do a lot of building if he reaches that 100,000, or if he reaches only 50 per cent of it. I am going to say to him that if he achieves 75 per cent of his estimate he will be doing a good job- provided, of course, he sees that decent houses are built. I think the need for housing in this country is greater today than it has been for some years past, and there are several reasons for this. First is the rapid increase in population with the resultant increase in all family formations. This, combined with immigration, has created a tremendous housing problem.
Then there is the obsolescence of existing units. Many houses are deteriorating at a very fast rate. I was interested in hearing the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) tell us about the wonderful houses which had been built at the beginning of the war and how well they had stood up. I know the hon. member is not a betting man and neither am I, but if he were I would bet him ten dollars that I could show him houses within two miles of this building which have practically collapsed-if they have not, it is a miracle. I refer to the houses over in Hull.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
We should benefit from
experience. It is not often that I have spoken critically of the government's housing program and I am hopeful that the minister will accept criticism a bit more readily than his predecessor, providing the criticism is not destructive. We should turn our attention to some of the conditions that have been allowed to exist under the National Housing Act to see if some improvement cannot be made. My mind goes back to a housing project to which I have referred on other occasions, the one carried out by the Bow River Construction Company. I should like to indicate some ways in which past failures could be prevented.
First, there was never a trusteeship set up for the down payments that were made. I raised this question about two years ago when I pointed out that it was wrong to permit people to make deposits on houses to a real estate agent or builder who could spend the money any way he liked. In some cases the contracts were not completed and the prospective home owners lost their down payments. I hope the minister is taking this under consideration and has made provision for a trusteeship to cover these down payments. The prospective home owners should have some protection for the money they pay in.
I am not laying all the mistakes that have been made on the doorstep of the government, although they are their responsibility. One other great mistake in the past was the lack of proper supervision. I know that the minister cannot go around and personally inspect all these buildings, but when I spoke on this question four or five years ago I pointed out that this was one of the great mistakes that were being made. I can recall at the moment one instance where an inspector accepted a house for the government in which inferior lumber filled with knotholes had been used for the floors. The floors were completely covered with paper, this inspector admitted that he had not seen them, yet he passed the house as being No. 1.
National Housing Act
These are mistakes which the government can avoid without any additional expense. When the government lets a contract it should see to it that the builder is properly qualified both from the financial point of view and in experience. That condition was not insisted upon in the past. I have here a booklet entitled, "The Integrated Housing Plan", which has been put out by the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation. I should like to know if the government recognizes this booklet as being authentic? I should like the minister to indicate whether people can place reliance in this booklet which I got just the other day.

speechtext: Who printed it?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: It is sent out by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, Ottawa, Canada, and is marked, "RCM-3". Apparently the minister has not yet given his approval to this and I do not know whether he intends to. Is this authentic, Mr. Minister?

speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: I should like to know before 1 quote from it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Under "credit" it states:
The builder's credit rating must be sound,-
That would be sound.
-and he must satisfy the lending institution and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that he is able, both financially and by virtue of experience, to undertake large-scale building operations.
Then I should like to refer to the builder's qualifications. Apparently this pamphlet is being sent out to prospective buyers all across the country. It is a government publication, but in the past this government has let contracts to persons who did not know the first thing about building. I do not think I can give a better example than that of the Bow River Construction Company. Speaking from memory, this company was given a credit rating by Central Mortgage of over $125,000, and I think I am conservative in making that estimate. The president of the company told me that they had not one cent to start with, and they certainly had no building experience whatever.
It is things like these that have caused difficulty. It is things like these that the government can correct without spending one cent. In most cases where building failures have occurred it will be found that they were due to negligence through lack of proper inspection. When people receive government pamphlets like this they put a great deal of confidence in them, and they should be able to do so. When they have the government's word that they have employed a competent

National Housing Act
contractor to build the houses the people naturally expect that their investment will be safeguarded, and they should have every reason to expect that. When I am speaking of failures, hon. members may think the project undertaken in Calgary by the Bow River Construction Company was the only one, but there have been others. There have been failures in Halifax, in Vancouver, in Winnipeg and in Toronto. However, I believe the Bow River construction failure was perhaps outstanding, and I spoke on it at some length in this house. I should have thought the government would have benefited from that criticism, but I was amazed when I read the Ottawa Journal of Thursday, September 29, and saw this heading: "Have down payment on homes held in trust, judge suggests." I was interested in the heading and I read on:
Toronto, September 29 (CP). Judge Ian Macdon-nell, presiding at a judicial inquiry into the failure of the big suburban Pelmo Park housing project, suggested yesterday legislation providing that down payments by home purchasers be kept in trust, may be a means of preventing similar losses.
I heartily endorse that recommendation; it is something I suggested a long time ago. Then the dispatch goes on:
Judge Macdonnell said that although there are many other cases of builders failing to complete homes after receiving money for them, "it is not illegal ... it may have to be cured by some trustee provisions."
An auditor's report yesterday disclosed that the Kershaw Construction Company, whose Pelmo Park housing project failed last May, had a deficit of $135,051 during the previous eight months.
Then notice this:
Fifty-four would-be home owners lost a total of $93,553 on the project.
Just because this government failed to accept criticism in the spirit in which it was offered over a year ago, more than $93,000 was lost by those people who invested all their savings in order to get homes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: That was a provincial company.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
I don't care what kind of company it was; that practice is carried on by this government under the National Housing Act. The next heading is, "Depositors lose all," and the article states:
The auditor's report said the total assets of the company-$86,700-did not represent anything any of the 54 depositors could realize.
So the assets were in such form that the down payments of the purchasers could not be recovered in any way. However, when I remember the estimates made by Central Mortgage and Housing with respect to the Bow River Construction Company, and remember that the president told me they did not have a red cent to start with, I am

just a little doubtful of that estimate of $86,700.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
You sold
them too well on the social credit theory.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
I do not know what that has to do with this; but my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) says this is Liberalism in practice. Now, Mr. Speaker, I am hopeful that the government will benefit by these past experiences. Speaking of these failures, I want to make one other point. This may not come under the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters), but at least it concerns him. I believe provision should be made in our legislation so that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could be prosecuted in the ordinary provincial courts. I took up this question some time ago with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), who agreed that there should be some court where both the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and-I was going to say the Manufacturers Life-these other institutions could be jointly prosecuted. As it stands today, when you have Central Mortgage and Housing in partnership with a lending institution, no matter how disreputable that lending institution may be, there is no place where those two bodies may be prosecuted. We had a good example of that in Calgary. When we tried to bring them before the court the judge said, "Oh, you cannot prosecute Central Mortgage and Housing in the provincial courts. They are a little god unto themselves, and you must go down to the exchequer court." Then the minister stood up here and said they were a little god unto themselves, and we could not prosecute them without their consent. So there we were stuck. How does the ordinary man get justice? I remember someone saying here the other day that you could find justice if you had the money to pay for it. That may be somewhat exaggerated, but certainly there are cases in which the ordinary man cannot get justice, and this is one of them. I have a great deal of hope for the new minister, though I will tell you in a year or so how it works out. I do trust that he will make some provision under which the courts of this land will be made available to those who are investing their money in these homes.
I hope I am wrong, but I am a little afraid that, with all the emphasis being laid on co-operation with the provinces, the dominion may be endeavouring to get out from under these embarrassing questions and pass them over to the provinces. I believe the suggestions now advanced may ultimately result in a good system of co-operation, if the proper steps are carefully taken.

Let me speak for a moment about low rental housing. One of the things proposed by the minister in his speech of September 21 was the lowering of the down payment by one-sixth. That is going to assist some people to come in under these housing projects. That one-sixth, of course, has to do with the difference between the cost of the house and the amount of the loan. It will be of great assistance in reducing the down payment, and to that extent will be a benefit; but the point I particularly want to mention right now is the purchase price. In the little pamphlet I referred to a moment ago it is mentioned that the price must be fair and reasonable and in his speech the minister emphasized that point. This brings me to the matter referred to the other day by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), when he emphasized the sanctity of contracts. I like that expression; but no government in this country has had less regard for the sanctity of contracts than this government under the National Housing Act as administered by the former minister. I want to repeat that; no government has had less regard for the sanctity of contracts than this federal government under the National Housing Act, as administered by the former minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Illustrate.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Illustrate? Let me refer to the contracts that were let in Calgary, which ranged anywhere from $6,600 to $8,125. Now, the end price was set; the contract was drawn up; the mortgage was drawn up; and everything was fixed including the escalator clause and the maximum of it was set, too. Then, when the people who bought those houses and signed those mortgages and contracts asked the government to fulfil that agreement, the government said: We have nothing to do with it. All they were asking was that the government abide by the contract. The government itself had set that price. These men had the contracts literally thrown in their face, and they lost all the money they put into them. When we talk about the sanctity of contracts, let us make that apply to this government as well as to any other concern in the country.
I am leaving out about seventy-five per cent of my notes, Mr. Speaker, because my time is running short. I shall have to take those matters up in committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Give us some more of those illustrations.
National Housing Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Yes, I want to refer to that illustration. I should like to go back and read some more from Judge Ian Macdonnell's statement of Thursday, September 29.
Angus McClaskey, the Ontario regional supervisor of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, said his organization put up twenty-five per cent of the first mortgages on the Pelmo homes.
He said the corporation has been faced with this type of problem for two years and "has come to the conclusion that the solution does not lie in the relationship between the purchaser and the mortgage company."
"We feel that as a corporation we cannot undertake to police vendor-purchaser transactions. We think this matter lies within the field of provincial legislation."
At this point, may I ask, is it any wonder I am suspicious? This is one of the supervisors of Central Mortgage and Housing, one of the officials concerned with the provincial-federal relationship, who is trying to get out from under some of the difficulties.
The article continues:
"Possibly there should be amendments to the Mechanics' Lien Act or in a licensing system for builders."
This is passing the buck to the provinces.
May I stop at this point to indicate one of the other recommendations I made a few years ago-when I mentioned it to the minister he said he was going to give consideration to it but whether he has, I do not know-and it was this: When we have contractors handling millions of dollars, then I believe those contractors should be bonded. They should not be licensed, they should be bonded. If that action were taken, it would not cost the government any more, even if the government had to pay the bonding fee. It would relieve the government of a great deal of responsibility because the bonding company would see to it that the conditions of the contract were carried out.
Mr. McClaskey said it would be impractical for the crown corporation to hold money in trust for would-be home owners.
Now, that is quite contradictory to what Judge Macdonnell recommends, and contradictory to what I believe is in the minister's mind. Mr. McClaskey does not think it feasible to provide a trusteeship for these down payments, and in that I strongly disagree with him.
He said the corporation tried to do this in conjunction with its integrated housing program for veterans. Under this plan, money from purchasers is held in trust. Builders are required to give the corporation a waiver on all liens, . . .
and so on.
I come to this question, Mr. Speaker, of reducing costs. It does seem to me that these houses are costing more money than is necessary when they are built on a large scale.

National Housing Act
There is a difference between a private contractor who is building a house, or perhaps two houses, and a man who is building twenty, forty or fifty houses. There is a great deal of difference in the cost of operation, for instance, in digging the basements. There is a great difference between having a machine come to dig fifty basements at once and having a machine come to dig one basement at a time. In large-scale operations a profit of $500 per unit is a tremendous amount. A great deal of money can be made at that rate. Five hundred dollars' profit for a contractor on a single unit is not too large. I would not think it was out of line at all, but of course it would depend on the type of house.
By means of research in the construction field, we could find new methods of construction. I could point some out to you, but my time is slipping by. Proper building inspection could be provided, and it would materially lower the costs to the government and the builder. Then, we could have proper control of the financing. I refer particularly to the mismanagement of finance by the lending institutions. I shall not dwell on it at this point, except to say that some of these lending institutions-I was going to say appropriate money, but that would not be the right term-are confiscating money which belongs to the purchaser for which the lending institution has never performed one bit of work. I do not think that should be permitted. I shall deal with that at length on another occasion.
I believe there is another point at which we could very well lower the cost of housing, and that is by the government cutting out some of these burdensome sales taxes which apply to items used in home construction. I believe, Mr. Speaker, the government could well afford to do that and the country would appreciate it. I believe the builders, too, would benefit if this government were to appoint a royal commission to investigate housing. I know the minister's answer to that, because I have it before me in the form of a press statement. He does not intend to appoint a royal commission. I have a clipping of the editorial before me, but I shall not bother to read it. It refers to the Canadian Construction Association and Ottawa building contractors who do not appreciate having a royal commission investigate this matter. Despite those two objections, I do not know whether the minister is very determined in his viewpoint. I believe there is a good deal of advantage in having a royal commission investigate the housing problem. Because it is so urgent that we have homes for our people to live in, because it is a financial problem and the government and the taxpayers indirectly have such a large financial 
investment in this project, I believe it would be well worth having a royal commission look into these housing projects.
I intended to speak at some length, Mr. Speaker, on low-rental projects. A great majority of the people in this country cannot afford to pay the rents that are being required. You know it is a strange thing that the people who live in the poorest houses in Canada receive an income so low that the low rents of today are simply far beyond their reach. This housing problem with which we are faced today is not going to be solved by the type of house that is being built today. I have not the time to go into that matter, however.
Perhaps I could just take one moment to read a section from this circular which I received from the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities. It contains the views of that organization on low-rental housing.
The federation, over the years, and more urgently during recent years, has urged the federal government to initiate a national program of subsidized low-rental housing. It again points out, that, as of the moment, the federal authorities, themselves, estimate that there are 300,000 more family units in Canada than there are houses to accommodate them. The great bulk of these families are low and average wage income families.
Moreover, according to a recent survey of the dominion bureau of statistics, nearly two-thirds of the urban tenants of Canada were paying less than $30 a month; of these, about one-half were paying less than $20 a month; and 5 per cent were paying less than $10.
Measured in terms of the demonstrable unmet need for housing accommodation; and the rentpaying capacity of those who comprise a major part of the population; there can be no question that the greatest housing need in Canada today is that for low-wage income families. Unable to afford the economic rents of new housing at the prevailing high construction costs, their housing needs cannot be met save by some form of subsidized housing.
May I interject and say that I agree with them wholeheartedly. Then they go on;
Meanwhile, the housing problem worsens for low-wage income families. Less and less housing accommodation is available to them because the proportion of new family formations is greater among them than among any other economic groups. With no new housing at all being constructed for low-wage families, congestion becomes greater and greater and conditions, already deplorable, become completely intolerable. The situation has reached the point where any further delay in at least a start on low-rental housing projects can only be regarded as a national calamity.
I think that is sufficient to show what an organization such as the national executive committee and advisory board of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities has to say about this condition and it requires no further explanation from me to show how great a need there is for this emergency housing program. I am aware that the minister appreciates all these things. I

am aware that he knows of these conditions because I think they prevail in abundance down in his own neighbourhood. And there are many of those conditions in the rest of Canada. But sympathy is not enough. It is going to take a great deal of daring on the minister's part. He is probably going to have to step away from those old conservative ideas which the former minister of reconstruction had; and he is going to have to be a little bit more liberal in his views and actions. I have great hopes that the present minister will do something to meet the situation. Time alone will tell.

speechtext:
I had
also intended, Mr. Speaker, to speak at some length tonight. In view of what has already been said, however, I shall restrict my remarks to about five minutes, and I shall keep to the resolution and to the statements which the minister made tonight. I feel that the minister took a step-true, it was a faltering and hesitant step; it was a cautious, and even ambiguous step; but it may have been a step.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Forward or backward?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
I hope it was forward. One had to examine his statement carefully, but I think the step he took was a forward one. It seems to me that in this debate on the resolution, and on the bill when it comes up for discussion, we must keep one fact in mind, namely, that in 1945, according to the government's own advisory committee, there was a shortage of 750,000 homes; and that, according to the statement the minister made some weeks ago, approximately the same shortage still exists. In other words, little progress has been made in meeting the backlog.
I assume that the statement which the minister made today, and the resolution that he has placed before us, is the government's answer to the housing problem. I think it is fair for hon. members tonight to ask themselves and to ask the minister this question: Does this resolution, or does the bill which is to be introduced, offer any tangible solution to the housing problem which is facing us? I hope it does, but from the minister's language tonight I am not quite sure. For instance, the minister said:
The legislation which we intend to introduce is of an enabling character . . . We have no knowledge of the extent to which provincial governments will participate in arrangements contemplated by the legislation . . .
What does that mean? Does it not mean that before any action on housing can be taken the various provincial legislatures will have to be called together? That may be four, five or six months from now. Then if any action is to be taken, each of those
National Housing Act
legislatures must approve and give leadership. In other words, the minister is leaving the prime responsibility up to the various provincial governments; and it looks to me- although I may be wrong-as though action might not be taken until late next spring, if ever, because some of the provincial governments may not be financially able, or may not desire, to take such action on housing.
Exactly what is the government proposing in this resolution? I think there are two main proposals. First of all, the minister is proposing in effect that the down payment should be cut in half. I want to say at once that I think many citizens will welcome this step because formerly they found it difficult to finance the down payment. But the lower down payment is going to mean higher carrying or interest charges, and in the final analysis it is also going to mean a higher cost to the purchaser. The lower down payment simply means a higher mortgage, and many Canadians today cannot even handle the mortgage charges which national housing has at the present time.
Then there is this additional factor, as I understand it, in the province of Ontario. I understand that Premier Frost and his government have for some time carried second mortgages.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: For two and a half years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
If I have read newspaper reports correctly, Premier Frost is now suggesting that, when this legislation goes through, the Ontario government will discontinue the practice of carrying second mortgages. What does this mean? It means that the average citizen in Ontario, which is the most populous province of Canada, and the province where the housing situation is most acute, is not going to be any better off with regard to the down payment than he was before. What the federal government is taking over, the Ontario government is leaving off. I therefore suggest that one of the main proposals of this resolution may not be effective. The second major proposition which the minister suggests is this. He says:
The arrangements provide that if any proposed project is deemed to be reasonable, the dominion will be prepared to proceed with the provinces in land assembly, the building of houses for sale, and the erection of rental housing either on an economic or a subsidized basis.
I was pleased tonight to hear the minister, and through him the government, at last use the word "subsidized". I hope it means what it purports to mean. I hope that the government really is anxious to do something about subsidized housing; although, as I said when I started, the phrasing is so ambiguous that it is hard to tell. I do not know whether

National Housing Act
the legislation which the minister is contemplating is going to mean a great many more houses for Canada. Certainly the minister was rather dubious on September 21 when he introduced the legislation. As he is reported at page 121 of Hansard, he said:
No one can estimate the amount of additional housing which these proposals will create.
Then he went on to say:
The measures proposed today should be helpful.
I would think they should be or why would he be bringing them before the house? He goes on to say:
They may have the effect of increasing the total number of completions.
They may have, he says. Was there ever such a lack of enthusiasm on the part of a minister when bringing in legislation to meet an acute and desperate problem? If there was, I have not seen it. The minister seems to be anything but enthusiastic. There was one other feature of the statement he made last September 21 which worried me a little. This is what he said about government policy:
The policy as enunciated by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply in 1946 is the keystone of our present policy: that Is, the creation of conditions favourable to a large housing program by private individuals and companies.
In other words, although the minister admits that private enterprise from 1945 to 1949 has not been able to solve our housing problem, he says that government policy is still the same. I am a little concerned, then. Surely by this time we can see that, if this housing problem is to be met, private enterprise must at least be supplemented by government spending on a substantial scale. The C.C.F. group would suggest a three-point program for improving the acute housing shortage. First we suggest a large-scale program of subsidized low-rental housing. I might say, as was pointed out earlier this evening by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), that we are not the only ones who have made such a proposal. The mayors association suggested it in 1947. The Canadian Legion suggested a similar program in 1948. The Canadian welfare council have proposed it. Many organizations have suggested low-rental subsidized housing on a substantial scale. I hope that the minister is prepared to embark on this type of housing but I am not sure-
