speechtext: Whose money would we use?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Partly federal government money.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: I thought it was C.C.F. money.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Many Liberal candidates suggested it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
In the second place, I -would suggest that private home building should be financed at interest rates of 2| per cent or less. Even in the United States, private home building is financed in many cases at 2 per cent or less. In New Zealand about 30,000 homes have been built and financed at interest rates of 1 per cent or 1J per cent. If New Zealand can do this I see no reason why Canada cannot do likewise. I believe the cost to the dominion government of borrowing money is between 2J per cent and 3 per cent at the present time. Certainly the money should be lent at least at cost, and not at 4J per cent as Central Mortgage and Housing are charging at the present time.
In the third place, Mr. Speaker, the C.C.F. group suggests that some genuine effort should be made to bring down construction costs. I think it is feasible that, by large-scale housing projects, construction costs could be reduced. The Canadian Congress of Labour suggested it the other day.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Would you bring down the price of hardware?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Yes, bring that down also. I was interested to note a reply which the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) gave, when he was asked to investigate the high cost of housing. According to the Canadian Press-and I quote the Montreal Star-the minister said this. The heading is: New Housing Inquiry Plea Rejected Winters Says Problem Closely Watched
How gratified those Canadians who have been living in two or three rooms since 1945 will be to note that the problem is being watched. We think that more effective action should be taken. Let me say that we welcome the steps which the minister has suggested tonight. They are the first tangible steps we have seen any member of the government take recently, but we do not feel that they are yet the answer to the housing problem which is facing this country.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Some of us had hoped that the minister might make some reply to the remarks that have been uttered in the house tonight. He has not done so, and for that reason I take it that it is necessary to ask some of the questions that were indicated in the remarks of hon. members tonight. What policy is the government going to adopt in regard to rent control?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: I am not in a position to enunciate government policy. That is a matter that will be announced in due course by the appropriate member of the government, one of my colleagues.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Is the house, either at the resolution stage or at a later stage on the bill, not to be told what the government's policy is to be in regard to rent control? Are we to be expected to deal with apparently the one measure in regard to housing that the government intends to bring in at this session, legislation that is to have a direct bearing on the building of houses for rent, without having any indication given to us as to the policy, if any, of the government, in regard to tne continuation of rent control? Everybody throughout the country is asking; what is the government's policy on rent control? Tenants are asking it; landlords are asking it; provincial governments are asking it; and this government maintains a sphinx-like silence. National Housing Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS

I should like to ask the minister a question as to who is allowed to buy or rent a house from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. There seems to be some difference in different sections where these houses are put up. I know of veterans who served overseas for five years, who have had their names in from one to three years or more, and who have not yet received
National Housing Act
houses. These are veterans with two or more children. Still they have not houses, while others who have come from outside have been given them. That does not seem right.
I have complained to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in my own constituency and also here in Ottawa, but have received no satisfaction. There should be provision for the veterans. I have in mind one case where the veteran has had his application in for two or three years, and has been refused a house. He has been told that he will have to go to the wartime prices and trade board and get a notice from them saying that he has to get out of the house he is in. Despite the fact that Central Mortgage knows that he has had notice from his landlord to get out, they say that he must get this notice from the wartime prices and trade board. Must veterans be put out on the street before they can obtain these houses? It looks to me as though there is a lot of favouritism going on, and the veterans feel that way also. Can the minister tell the committee what the regulations are in regard to this matter and if they are the same throughout Canada?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
There is a point-rating system which has been carried on throughout this entire operation and which is subject to close scrutiny by the Canadian Legion. So far as I know, this system is acceptable to the Legion and 1 have yet to hear of an instance where the Legion has said that there has been discrimination against any veteran. This pointrating system takes into consideration a man's service overseas, the number of children he has, the type of accommodation in which he is living, the length of time he has been in the district and other factors. Every effort is made to administer this system fairly in the interests of all concerned.
It is understandable that there will be those who feel that they have a high classification in one category, but when the over-all picture is viewed it is found that some other veteran has prior right to a vacant rental house. As I say, it has been administered fairly and I believe that belief is held by the Legion.

speechtext:
Office of the Prime Minister Province of Quebec
Quebec, October 26, 1949
The Right Honourable Louis S. St. Laurent,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa.

maintopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT-PROCEDURE IN AMENDMENTS FURTHER CORRESPONDENCE WITH PREMIERS OF PROVINCES
speechtext:
I have submitted today to my colleagues of the executive council of the province the letter which you forwarded to me under date of October 21 and which I have received Monday morning the 24th.
In your letter you say:
"It seems to me that we have both made our positions very clear and that it would not serve any useful purpose to continue our correspondence until such time as we are in a position to extend invitations to the provincial governments to confer with us on this subject."
Indubitably our respective positions have been made "very clear" The government of the province of Quebec reiterates the statements made in the letters which I sent you under date of September 21st last and October 5th and 19th instant.
As you are no doubt aware, our legislature usually undertakes in January to give consideration to the very important measures on the program of our annual session. Will you kindly let me know when the Canadian intergovernmental conference which you propose to call in order to deal with constitutional matters is to be held?
This information is necessary to us, and we should like to have it as soon as possible.
Yours sincerely,
M. L. Duplessis
Office of the Prime Minister Canada
Ottawa, October 29, 1949 Hon. Maurice L. Duplessis, M.L.A.,
Premier of Quebec,
Quebec, Que.
My dear Premier:
I have submitted your letter of the 26th instant to my colleagues in the government and we feel that it would be desirable to hold the proposed dominion-provincial conference to consider a method of amending the constitution in Canada early in the new year.
Since other provincial governments, like the government of Quebec, will no doubt wish to make plans for their legislative sessions, I am writing today to the premiers of all the provinces suggesting that the conference begin its sessions on Tuesday, January 10, 1950, if that date appears to be generally convenient.
I should be pleased to have your views on this point.
Yours sincerely,
Louis S. St. Laurent

My dear Premier:

I have replied today to Mr. Duplessis suggesting that the conference begin its sessions on Tuesday, January 10, 1950, if that date appears to be generally convenient.
I should be pleased to have your views on this point.
Yours sincerely,
Louis S. St. Laurent
